NJ Gaming Revenue Rises 6.3% in October Despite Pressures

Published November 18, 2026 · 3 min read · By the OddsLighthouse Editorial Team

New Jersey's casinos, sportsbooks, and online gaming operators posted $649.5 million in total gaming revenue in October 2026, up 6.3% from $611.1 million a year earlier, according to data from the state's Division of Gaming Enforcement. Through the first ten months of 2026, cumulative revenue reached $6.04 billion, a 5.2% increase over the same stretch of 2025.

Where the growth is coming from

Internet gaming, New Jersey's online casino segment, remains the fastest-growing piece of the market. It brought in $287.4 million in October, up 10.4% from $260.3 million the year before, and has grown 12.9% year-to-date to $2.69 billion. Atlantic City's nine land-based casino hotels posted $245.9 million for the month, up 4.7% year over year, with a slimmer 1.8% year-to-date gain to $2.48 billion. Sports betting was the laggard: October gross revenue of $116.3 million was essentially flat against $116.1 million a year earlier, and the segment's year-to-date total is actually down 5.5%, to $864.6 million from $914.6 million. The state collected $94.3 million in gross gaming revenue taxes in October and $851.1 million for the year to date.

Regulatory pressure in the background

The revenue growth comes as New Jersey regulators and lawmakers push on two fronts that could reshape the market. In September, the Assembly's Tourism, Gaming and the Arts Committee approved a resolution aimed at stopping operators from using targeted advertising to reach people at risk of gambling-related harm, though it leaves open exactly how at-risk individuals would be identified. Separately, the state's Attorney General's Office has asked the US Supreme Court to overturn an appellate ruling that found only the Commodity Futures Trading Commission can oversee Kalshi's prediction-market activity — a decision that, if left standing, would place sports-related prediction contracts outside New Jersey's own gambling jurisdiction. The state argues those contracts are sports betting by another name and should be regulated accordingly.

Why it matters to NJ players

For bettors and casino players in the state, the headline number is a sign the broader market keeps growing even as one of its segments — sports betting — cools off relative to last year. The online casino side's continued double-digit growth suggests operators are still successfully shifting volume toward iGaming, while the flat-to-declining sports betting figures line up with a broader slowdown several other states have reported this fall. The pending Supreme Court question on prediction markets is the bigger wildcard: however it resolves, it will help determine whether New Jersey keeps the same regulatory reach over sports-adjacent contracts that it has over its licensed sportsbooks today.
